intro: Pronouns replace a noun so you don't repeat it: she, him, us, them… English has one form for the subject (I) and one for the object (me), and the object pronoun always comes after the verb (I love him).
objectifs: Know the seven subject pronouns and the seven object pronouns.
Put the object pronoun after the verb or after a preposition.
Choose between he, she, it and they for a person, an animal or a thing.
Avoid the traps: It's me, Me too, my friend and I, the order “give it to me”.

texte: The subject pronoun does the action; it goes before the verb. The object pronoun receives the action; it goes after the verb or after a preposition (with, for, to, at…).
Two pronouns don't change: “you” (subject and object) and “it”. The others have two forms to learn.
sections.note: “I” always has a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence: Yesterday I… But “me” has a small letter.

texte: In some languages the object pronoun goes before the verb. In English, it ALWAYS goes after the verb: I see her, He helps us. Never say “I her see”.
After a preposition, use the object form too: with me, for her, to them, about us, between you and me. Don't say “with I” or “for she”.
In English, things have no gender: a table, a car, a city are all “it”. For a beautiful house, say “It's beautiful”.
For an animal you don't know, say “it”. For a pet you know, people often say “he” or “she”. For a person, don't say “it”: if you don't know if a baby is a boy or a girl, say “they” or “he or she”.
“They” is also used for one person when you don't know their gender, or when they prefer this pronoun: Someone is at the door. What do they want? The verb stays plural: they are.
exemples: I love this city. It's so lively!
Where's my phone? — It's on the table.
We've got a cat. She's ten years old.
A customer called. They want a refund.

sections.titre: Traps: It's me, Me too, my friend and I
texte: After “to be”, in normal English, use the object form: “Who's there? — It's me.” “It is I” exists but is very formal and old-fashioned.
To react, say “Me too” and “Me neither”, never “I too”. Don't repeat the subject with “me”: not “Me, I like tea”, but “I like tea” (stress I) or “Personally, I like tea”.

When you talk about yourself and another person, put yourself last to be polite: “my friend and I” as a subject, “my friend and me” as an object. Tip: remove the other person to check (I went → my friend and I went; for me → for my friend and me).
exemples: My sister and I live in Montréal.
She invited my husband and me.

texte: With verbs like give, send, show, tell and bring, there can be two objects: the thing and the person. With two nouns, you can say “Give Ana the book” or “Give the book to Ana”.
When the thing is a pronoun (it, them), normally put the thing first, then “to” + person: Give it to me. “Give me it” is heard in informal British English, but “Give it to me” is always safe.
exemples: Can you send me the photos? — Sure, I can send them to you tonight.

formule: Subject + verb + object: I · you · he · she · it · we · they → me · you · him · her · it · us · them
prononciation: Object pronouns are often weak and unstressed: I like him /aɪ ˈlaɪk ɪm/ (the h often disappears), Call her /ˈkɔːl ə/, Tell them /ˈtel ðəm/.
Stress them only for emphasis or contrast: I love HER, not HIM.
“them” /ðem/ starts with /ð/ (tongue between the teeth, voice on). Don't say “dem” or “zem”.
“us” /ʌs/ has an unvoiced s. “he” /hiː/ has a breathed h: hear the difference between “he's” /hiːz/ and “is” /ɪz/.
“her” is /hɜː/ strong, /ə/ weak; “him” is /hɪm/ strong, /ɪm/ weak.
erreurs: The object pronoun goes after the verb.
Where's the car? — She's in the garage.
A thing = it, not he / she.
Me and my brother are tired.
My brother and I are tired.
As a subject, and to be polite: “my brother and I”.
I prefer tea. / Personally, I prefer tea.
English doesn't repeat the subject with “me”.

dialogue.contexte: Two friends prepare a birthday party for their flatmate in their flat in Lyon.
lignes: Is the cake ready? Paul loves chocolate. I'm sure he'll love it.
Yes, it's in the fridge. Where are the candles? I can't find them.
They're in my bag. Here, take them.
Yes, they are. I'm meeting them at the station. And his sister is coming with us to the restaurant.
them, us after a verb or preposition.
Great! I like her a lot.
Me too. Shh! Someone's at the door. Is it him?
Hi, it's me! Why is it so dark in here?

mots: make it easier for someone to do something
Send it to me by email.
They often invite us for dinner.
ask someone to come to an event
go to see a person or a place

exercices.consigne: Replace the words in brackets with a pronoun.

items: My friend and (I / me) live in Ghent.
Where's my umbrella? — (It / She) is by the door.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Correct it.
items: I don't like coffee. / Personally, I don't like coffee.

exercices.consigne: Complete the second sentence with the right object pronoun.
items: Marc is very nice. I like ___.
We need help. Can you help ___?
My grandparents are lonely. She talks to ___ every day.
That's my pen! Give ___ to me, please.

exercices.consigne: Write four sentences about people and things that are important to you. Use at least four different object pronouns.
items: My grandmother lives in Bafoussam. I call her every Sunday. My cousins often visit us in summer, and we take them to the beach. I've got an old guitar; I play it every evening.

a_retenir: Subject / object: I-me, you-you, he-him, she-her, it-it, we-us, they-them.
The object goes after the verb (I see her) or after a preposition (with us).
A thing = it. A person whose gender you don't know = they (+ are).
It's me · Me too · my friend and I (subject) / my friend and me (object).
Give it to me: the thing (pronoun) first, then to + person.
